name: Pegvisomant
lead: Pegvisomant, sold as Somavert, is a pegylated growth hormone (GH) analog that blocks the GH receptor. [1][2] It is approved in the US for acromegaly in patients who responded inadequately to surgery or radiation, or for whom those are unsuitable, with the treatment goal of normalizing IGF-1. [2]

Its link to appearance is through the GH and IGF-1 axis. Acromegaly, the condition it treats, produces enlargement of the hands, feet and facial features, and by lowering IGF-1 the drug is used to control that overgrowth, which is why it is sometimes mentioned in height and appearance forums as a GH-axis compound that works in the opposite direction to GH boosters. [3][4] No published trial tests it for cosmetic purposes in people without GH excess. [3][4]

Wikipedia credits its discovery to John Kopchick and graduate student Wen Chen at Ohio University in 1987, with the FDA approving it for acromegaly in 2003 and Pfizer marketing it. [12] Documented risks in the label include hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes, liver toxicity, lipohypertrophy and systemic hypersensitivity. [2]

paras: The US label indication is acromegaly after inadequate response to surgery or radiation, or when those are not appropriate. [2] Grokipedia describes a pediatric use in pituitary gigantism as investigational. [1] A phase 3 study of children with growth hormone excess has been registered. [5]

A 12-week randomized double-blind study in 112 acromegaly patients tested three pegvisomant doses against placebo, and a long-term study followed 160 patients for an average of 425 days. [3][4] Grokipedia reports IGF-1 normalization in most patients over the long term. [1] The ACROSTUDY surveillance reviewed 1288 subjects for long-term safety. [6] The 2000 New England Journal of Medicine study tested 10, 15 and 20 mg daily doses against placebo for 12 weeks in 112 patients, and the 2001 Lancet study of 160 patients measured tumour volume by MRI together with serum GH and IGF-1 in 152 of them. [3][4] A 2000 multicenter randomized study of six patients resistant to octreotide tested pegvisomant as an alternative, [13] a 2005 Lancet study examined combining somatostatin analogues with weekly pegvisomant, [8] and a 2009 trial examined successful weekly administration. [14] The German Pegvisomant Observational Study evaluated safety and efficacy in clinical practice. [15] A 2025 consensus statement on acromegaly outcomes and a 2021 Pituitary Society update to management guidelines place pegvisomant among the available medical therapies. [16][17]

The label lists hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes, liver toxicity (transaminase elevations above ten times the upper limit were reported in a small share of patients), cross-reactivity with GH assays, lipohypertrophy and systemic hypersensitivity. [2] Animal studies showed fetotoxicity at a high dose and human pregnancy data are insufficient. [2]

Pegvisomant binds GH receptors and blocks endogenous GH signaling, which lowers serum IGF-1 and other GH-responsive proteins. [2] It is a 191-amino-acid recombinant protein with attached polyethylene glycol, which changes its pharmacokinetics. [1][7] Because it blocks the receptor rather than suppressing secretion, GH assays may be unreliable during treatment. [2]

The drug was designed by altering human GH so that it binds the receptor without triggering signalling, and PEGylation, the attachment of polyethylene glycol, extends its time in the circulation; a review of PEGylation in biological therapies describes the approach in general terms. [7][12] It is produced in genetically modified E. coli according to Wikipedia. [12] Because it blocks action at the receptor, IGF-1, not GH, is the marker followed during treatment, and IGF-1 assay performance has been reviewed. [2][18]

Randomized and long-term studies have been performed in acromegaly. [3][4][6][8] Registered studies also cover bone microarchitecture in acromegaly, quality of life, children with GH excess, pre-diabetes and severe insulin resistance. [5][9][10][11] No studies were found of pegvisomant for cosmetic or height purposes in healthy people. A randomized study titled GH receptor antagonist treatment reduces exercise performance in young males examined the effect of blocking GH action in healthy young men, which is the closest published work to non-acromegaly use. [19] Wikipedia notes that some studies have suggested possible anti-tumour use in certain cancers but that this remains exploratory. [12]

Wikipedia describes the discovery of pegvisomant at Ohio University in 1987 by John Kopchick and graduate student Wen Chen, followed by FDA approval for acromegaly in 2003 and marketing by Pfizer. [12] A 2002 Endocrine Reviews article on the discovery, development and use of GH receptor antagonists covers the path from the molecular design of GH antagonists to use in patients. [20] Europe approved it in 2002, ahead of the United States. [1]

timeline.event: Discovered at Ohio University by John Kopchick and Wen Chen. [12]

Long-term Lancet study of 160 patients published. [4]

card.summary: Prescription GH-receptor blocker for acromegaly; its appearance relevance is as the opposite of a GH booster, and it has no cosmetic studies.
card.note: Approved only for acromegaly; label warns of liver toxicity and hypoglycemia in diabetes.

quick.overview:
Pegvisomant (Somavert) is an injectable drug that blocks the growth hormone receptor. It is approved for acromegaly, a condition of GH excess causing enlarged hands, feet and facial features.

It appears in appearance discussions as a GH-axis compound. No published study tests it for cosmetic use.
quick.mechanism: It binds the GH receptor and prevents GH from signaling, which lowers IGF-1.
quick.risks: The label lists liver enzyme elevations, hypoglycemia in diabetic patients, injection-site lipohypertrophy and hypersensitivity. It is prescription-only.

chain: Controls GH-driven overgrowth of hands, feet and facial features in acromegaly
angle.text: In acromegaly, excess GH enlarges facial features and extremities, and pegvisomant lowers IGF-1 so those effects are controlled rather than progressing. In people without GH excess it is not an appearance treatment, and its appearance in forums is as a GH-axis reference point.
